name: Ajië
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Ajië (ajie1238) is not in the catalog. The single target item, Kasarhérou/de la Fontinelle 1961 'Prosodèmes de la langue mélanésienne de Houaïlou' (BSL 56(1): 181–201), is a first-hand prosodic description of this language (relevance confirmed by Haudricourt's 1977 BSL review of the 1976 book, which names it as the first signalling of Houaïlou's 'type prosodique très particulier'), but no open copy exists: archive.org's BSL run skips 1939–1969, Gallica has no 1961 BSL, HathiTrust is search-only and blocked from our machine. Priority high. Screening the 17 open BSL volumes (1970–1979) on archive.org yielded two second-hand characterizations: Haudricourt 1974 (BSL 69(2): 315–316) — Houaïlou has 'ton glottal', not pitch tone, the marked glottalized prosodeme corresponding to marked high tone in Paicî/Cèmuhî and marked low tone in the far south — and Haudricourt 1977 (BSL 72(2), review 171) — the 1976 book's phonology (pp. 17–148) gives the full description by generation and dialect. Rivierre 1978 (BSL 73(1)) describes initial accent in Xârâcùù and is silent on Ajië. None states stress placement for Ajië, so best_new_statement is found=false. Best acquisition targets: de la Fontinelle 1976 (Harvard print, Scan & Deliver eligible; HathiTrust mdp.39015024001482 search-only) and the 1961 article (BSL 56, print); secondary: Tryon et al. 1995 A'jië sketch (DOI 10.1515/9783110884012.2.859, paywalled) and de la Fontinelle 1979. All fetched sources

new_statements.quote: Règle 1 L'accent d'intensité frappe la syllabe initiale des mots pleins. Les monosyllabes lexèmes le reçoivent également. Il n'est pas noté dans cette position au cours du présent travail : 'kai « manger des féculents » [p. 125] … 3.3. Cependant, l'accent n'est pas sur l'initiale dans certains cas : a) L'accent peut être réalisé sur la seconde syllabe ou la seconde more des syllabes longues : va'rui « lune » […] En synchronie, il est impossible de donner les raisons de cette place accentuelle : les lexèmes de ce type sont donc appris comme tels par les locuteurs. b) Par contre, l'accent se « justifie » par l'application de la règle 1 dans les innombrables composés. [p. 126]
new_statements.translation: Rule 1: The intensity accent strikes the initial syllable of full words. Lexical monosyllables receive it too. It is not marked in this position in the present work: 'kai 'eat starchy food' [p. 125] … 3.3. However, the accent is not on the initial syllable in certain cases: a) The accent may be realized on the second syllable, or the second mora of long syllables: va'rui 'moon' […] Synchronically it is impossible to give the reasons for this accent placement: lexemes of this type are therefore learned as such by speakers. b) By contrast, the accent is 'justified' by the application of Rule 1 in the innumerable compounds. [p. 126]

Les monosyllabes lexèmes le reçoivent également. Il n'est pas noté dans cette position au cours du présent travail : ' kai « manger des féculents >> ' pirixa ' piriya « espiègle >>> ' néxùrù...". q5.xml and q10.xml (both PA125) add the head "aux dépens des autres par la voix. Règle 1 L'accent d'intensité frappe la syllabe initiale des mots pleins"; q3.xml (PA125) gives the unaccented function-word examples and "Règle 2…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level intensity stress (accent d'intensité) falls on the first syllable of every full word (lexical word/radical), including lexical monosyllables; function words (mots-outils such as pronouns) are unstressed; in compounds the stress marks the radical, i.e. the beginning of the lexical element (p. 133: 'l'accent signale à l'auditeur le radical ou le début du monème'). A limited set of lexemes carry stress on the second syllable or second mora instead, unpredictably. Superimposed on this is a lexically placed 'accent glottalisé' (a glottal tone/accent, realized as an intensity accent with abrupt glottal closure) which may follow but never precede the intensity accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Discussed: two intensity accents cannot occupy contiguous syllables (p. 141); in words carrying a final glottalized accent, 'l'accent secondaire est l'accent démarcatif initial, l'accent primaire celui de la dernière more' (p. 132, e.g. 'aayo'o 'slug'); 'accent secondaire; cf. 3.19' mentioned for lexemes like daa'au (p. 126); accent-inducing suffixes (Règle 3, p. 127) can shift or add an accent, e.g. when the final syllable of the word is unaccented 'c'est l'antépénultième qui porte l'accent d'intensité' (p. 128).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexemes with accent on the second syllable/second mora (va'rui 'lune', daa'au 'abasourdi', ka'a 'chose'), learned as such; accent-inducing suffixes and suffix-driven shifts (§3.1x, pp. 127–128); function words unaccented; the older description by Leenhardt (1946, repeated in the 1961 BSL article) claimed instead a 'light tonic accent on the last syllable of the full word', which de la Fontinelle's description supersedes (the final prominence probably corresponds to her glottal accent / utterance-final demarcative accent).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/morpheme level: the rule is stated for 'mots pleins' (lexical words) and radicals within compounds, with a demarcative function; at utterance level an additional end-of-utterance demarcative accent falls on the last or penultimate syllable of the utterance (p. 144), and the intensity accent 'met en relief dans la chaîne les monosyllabes lexicaux et les éléments radicaux pleins' (Règle 2, p. 125). The author distinguishes this intensity accent from the 'accent glottalisé'/'ton glottal' (pp. 140–145), which Haudricourt (1974) treats as a glottal tone; Ajië is thus a stress language with a lexical glottal accent, not a musical-tone language.
new_statements.identity_note: de la Fontinelle 1976 describes 'la langue de Houaïlou' = A'jië (ajie1238), based on speakers from the Houaïlou region (a coastal 'bord de mer' consultant and older speakers; Haudricourt notes the description covers generations and dialects); Leenhardt's 'houaïlou' is the same language. No separate glottocode involved.

sources.citation: Haudricourt, André-Georges (1974). Compte rendu no. 177 of J.-C. Rivierre, Phonologie comparée des dialectes de l'extrême-sud de la Nouvelle-Calédonie (SELAF 1973). Bulletin de la Société de Linguistique de Paris 69(2): 315–316.
sources.quote: Or, dans la région intermédiaire, nous avons la langue Houailou, dont Mme de La Fontinelle vient de donner une description dans une thèse à l'impression, langue qui n'est pas à ton musical mais à ton glottal ; et il me semble bien que c'est ce ton glottal « marqué » qui correspond au ton marqué des langues à ton musical ; ainsi un arbre usuel le « gayac » Acacia spirorbis Lab. a un ton haut dans les langues du centre, glottalisé en Houailou, et bas à l'extrême-sud. [Translation: In the intermediate region we have the Houaïlou language, which Mme de la Fontinelle has just described in a thesis in press, a language that has not a musical (pitch) tone but a glottal tone; and it seems to me that this marked glottal tone corresponds to the marked tone of the pitch-tone languages; thus a common tree, the gaiac, has a high tone in the central languages, is glottalized in Houaïlou, and has low tone in the far south.]
sources.locator: BSL 69(2) 1974, comptes rendus, no. 177, pp. 315–316 (scanned lines 21396–21416 of the saved file)
sources.note: Second-hand (reporting de la Fontinelle's then-unprinted thesis) but the only explicit statement of Ajië's prosodic type read in this sweep: Houaïlou is not a pitch-tone language but has a 'glottal tone' — a marked glottalized prosodeme that corresponds to the marked high tone of the central languages (Paicî/Cèmuhî) and the marked low tone of the far south. No statement of where word stress falls.
